opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's something we ran into pretty directly with budget forcing in the s1 work. The basic idea is simple: when the model tries to end its thinking, you suppress the end-of-thinking token and append "Wait." That nudges the model to keep going, and often it'll go back, double-check its reasoning, and sometimes catch a mistake. So you do get this nice knob for scaling test-time compute.

But it doesn't scale forever. What we saw is that the first one or two "waits" can help quite a bit, and then the gains start to flatten out. If you keep pushing, eventually performance plateaus or even gets worse. The model starts going in circles: repeating itself, re-verifying things it already verified, or getting stuck in loops where it isn't adding new information. At some point you're also running into the context window, so there's a hard ceiling there too.

So I think about it in a couple of ways. One is that "wait" is a fairly crude intervention. It doesn't tell the model *what* to reconsider; it just says "don't stop yet." That works when there's latent useful reasoning the model would have done if it hadn't stopped early, but once that's exhausted, extra forcing is mostly noise. The other is that the model was only trained on reasoning traces of a certain length and style. Pushing it far beyond that distribution means you're asking it to do something it hasn't really learned to do well.

I see budget forcing as a nice, simple baseline that shows test-time scaling is possible even with a tiny amount of fine-tuning. But if you want to extrapolate much further, you probably need better methods: training the model to make use of longer contexts, smarter ways of deciding when to continue, or combining sequential thinking with parallel approaches like sampling multiple traces and aggregating them. That's where I think a lot of the interesting open questions are.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the first one or two “waits” can help and gains then flatten, but does not state consistent math gains through four insertions.

r002.rationale: The candidate mentions getting stuck in loops, but does not specify that more than four “waits” can cause an infinite loop.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we looked at pretty closely in the s1 work, because the budget forcing trick is really simple: when the model wants to stop, you just suppress the end-of-thinking token and append "wait," and it keeps going. And the natural question is, how far can you push that?

What we found is that it does scale, but it saturates. The first "wait" or two tend to help a lot. The model goes back, re-checks its arithmetic, catches a sign error, reconsiders an assumption. Accuracy on things like AIME and MATH500 goes up fairly cleanly as you extend the compute that way. But once you get to something like four, five, six "waits," the gains flatten out, and in some cases it starts to hurt.

And I think there are two reasons for that. One is just that the model has finite capacity to actually make use of extra tokens. If it's already verified the answer and it's confident, appending "wait" doesn't give it new information. It just forces it to generate more text, and what it tends to do is go into these loops where it re-derives the same thing, or it second-guesses a correct answer and flips to a wrong one. So you get this oscillation behavior, and the extra reasoning becomes noise rather than signal.

The second reason is the context window. Every "wait" adds tokens, and eventually you hit the limit and the model gets cut off, so you lose the ability to even extract a final answer. So there's a hard ceiling from the architecture, independent of whether the reasoning quality is still improving.

So the way I think about it is that budget forcing is a control knob, not a free lunch. It's great for giving you a controllable test-time scaling curve, which was really the point of s1 — showing you can get that curve with only a thousand examples of supervised fine-tuning. But the slope is limited by what the model has already learned to do with its thinking. Appending "wait" can't teach it a new strategy; it can only let it apply the strategies it already has more thoroughly. If you want to push the ceiling itself, you need better training, whether that's more or more carefully selected data, or reinforcement learning, so the model actually learns when extra verification is worth doing and when it should just commit.

And honestly, I think the more interesting direction is making the model decide this itself rather than us forcing it externally. "Wait" is a blunt instrument. Ideally the model has a calibrated sense of its own uncertainty and allocates the extra compute to the problems that need it.

r001.rationale: The response says math accuracy on AIME and MATH500 goes up fairly cleanly as compute is extended, with gains flattening around four to six waits.

r002.rationale: It describes repetitive loops and oscillation, but does not state that more than four waits can cause an infinite loop.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s probably a limit, but I wouldn’t think of it as a fixed number of times you can say “wait.” It’s more about whether the model still has something useful to do. If it’s checking an assumption or trying a different approach, extending the thinking can help. If it’s just repeating itself, more tokens aren’t buying you much, and you might even get it to second-guess a correct answer.

So I’d expect that limit to depend on the problem and the model. The interesting question is whether we can learn when to keep thinking and when to stop, instead of always forcing the same amount of extra computation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s probably a limit, but I wouldn’t think of it as a fixed number of “waits.” The question is whether the model is still doing useful computation. If it’s checking an assumption or trying a different approach, giving it more time can help. If it’s just repeating itself, another “wait” doesn’t really buy you anything.

So you’d want to look at performance as you increase the thinking budget. Does accuracy keep improving, or does it flatten out? And that limit could be different for different problems and different models. Ideally, the model would learn when more thinking is useful and when it should just give the answer.
